_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-15) first version, from latent-season7-bible-v1.0.1.md row a7e05 and writer brief a7e05-v1.0.0.md. Defence only: the failure (a rule that judges what text looks like, not what it means) is named and explained; no bypass, payload or example of text that slips past a check appears. a7e04's next field honoured (checks on what goes into and comes out of a model, with classifiers, policies and refusals that help without blocking the job). a5e03 recalled (measuring a check against labels). The night runs from the guardrail's switch-on at 17:00 on Tuesday 13 October to 06:00 on Wednesday 14 October; every tide request came after the coastguard's surge warning at 23:40, so the 14 refusals all fall on 14 October. Llama Guard paper and NeMo Guardrails page read 15 October 2026.
title: Guardrails

post.author: u/duty_pilot_hjalmar
post.title: I'm the night duty pilot at a harbour. On a storm-surge night our assistant refused 14 of 14 requests for the tides, and told every one of them nothing.

blocks.text: I'm Hjalmar, night duty pilot at Ardcarrow Harbour. A pilot is a local sailor who boards ships and steers them up the channel. At night I also answer the harbour's phone, the duty line.

Our website has an assistant, a chat box that answers questions. It runs on a language model, a program that reads text and writes text back. It gives tide times and berth details, where ships tie up. Shipping agents, the firms that arrange a ship's visit, can ask about their bills.

Agents first log in with a password. Each agent's account has a number in the account format: two letters and eight digits. Anyone holding it can ask our billing office about that firm's bills, so we keep it private.

Every month Ms Oyinlola, our systems officer, reads a sample of replies and marks what each one holds. A set marked like that is a labelled set. In September's 500, six replies gave a real account number to visitors not logged in. That is a leak: private data reaching the wrong person.

The assistant's instructions, the standing orders sent with every question, already kept bills for logged-in agents. But instructions only ask the model; they lock nothing. So she added a guardrail: a check in code that reads every reply before anyone sees it, and stops any that break its rule.
One that checks replies going out is an output guardrail. Her rule: block any reply with eight or more digits close together. A blocked reply becomes a refusal: I can't help with that.
She tested it on 50 made-up account numbers. It caught 50 of 50. At 17:00 on Tuesday 13 October it went live.

At 23:40 the coastguard radioed a surge warning. A storm surge is wind and low air pressure pushing the sea above the tide table: the day's high and low waters, each with a time and height. On a surge night we check the table hourly.
At 00:31 the duty line rang. Dragoslav, a shipping agent, said the assistant wouldn't give him today's tides. I read them from our printed tide book. Nobody else rang.
At 06:30 I opened the assistant's log, its record of every question. Each line below shows the time on 14 October, who asked, what for, and what the guardrail did.

00:12  visitor           full tide table  blocked: 8+ digits
00:29  agent, logged in  full tide table  blocked: 8+ digits
00:29  reply sent: I can't help with that.
... 12 more tide requests, the last at 05:10, all blocked
Fourteen people asked for the tides on a surge night. Fourteen were told nothing.
From 17:00 to 06:00 the log holds 40 requests: 14 for tides, 19 for berths and 7 about bills. All 14 tide requests wanted the full table, and only those were blocked. No reply held an account number.

Top row, the assistant's log from 17:00 on 13 October to 06:00 on 14 October: 40 requests; 14 full tide tables, all 14 blocked; 26 berth and billing requests, all answered, none holding an account number. Bottom row, before switch-on: the test, 50 made-up account numbers, 50 caught; September's labelled sample of 500 replies, 6 holding a real account number; 180 tide replies in that sample, 61 of them full tables.

blocks.text: A full table is four times and four heights in a row, like 03:12 5.8 09:31 1.2. To the rule, that is just digits close together. Most nights people ask for the next high water: six digits, which passes. Before last night nobody had been refused a tide.
The coastguard says the surge returns with tonight's high water. Ms Oyinlola is in at 08:00. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing at Ardcarrow is haunted. Your guardrail never read a tide table; it counted digits. A guardrail judges what text looks like, not what it means. Some are a fixed rule written in code, like yours. Others are a classifier: a small model trained on a labelled set to sort text into allowed or blocked. Either kind can stop an innocent reply along with a bad one, so a check needs checking against a person's labels, as Faithful or Fabricated (a5e03) did. A guardrail can also run watch only: it writes down what it would block and blocks nothing. Two questions. Before 17:00 on Tuesday, what was the rule tried on, besides the thing it should catch? And on September's 500, how many replies would it have stopped, and how many of those held an account number?

replies.author: u/duty_pilot_hjalmar
replies.text: Only the 50 made-up numbers. Ms Oyinlola ran the rule over September's 500 when she came in. It would have stopped 67: the 6 with account numbers, and 61 tide replies. September had 180 tide replies, and those 61 were the full tables. Stopping a reply that held a number is a catch; stopping an innocent one is a false alarm. So 6 catches and 61 false alarms.

comments.author: u/zero_leaks_fridtjof
comments.text: Six real leaks caught, none missed. That is a guardrail doing its job. A miss, a leak it lets through, can cost a firm its privacy and the harbour its good name. A wrong refusal costs someone a phone call. A guardrail that never misses is worth any number of false alarms. Safety first: keep it exactly as it is.

replies.author: u/duty_pilot_hjalmar
replies.text: One phone call would have been fine. Thirteen of the fourteen never rang; they got the refusal and nothing else. Two were our own pilots, who had the printed book aboard the launch, our pilot boat.

comments.author: u/ships_agent_dragoslav
comments.text: I'm the agent from 00:31. I had a sailing to plan for the morning high water. The assistant said it couldn't help, and nothing else: no page to try, no number to ring. I found the duty line in an old email.

replies.author: u/duty_pilot_hjalmar
replies.text: Our website's tide page has had the full table all along. The refusal never mentioned it.

reply.prompt: The surge returns with tonight's high water, and the guardrail is still on. What should Ardcarrow change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Switch the guardrail off for the storm and switch it back on once the surge passes.
options.verdict: A blind gap, then the same night
options.part2: Ms Oyinlola switched the guardrail off at 08:15. We replayed it in the sim. With it off, tonight's 40 requests get 0 refusals and every tide table goes out. But off means off for everyone: on September's traffic, all 6 account numbers reach visitors who are not logged in, 6 misses and 0 catches. And the plan was to switch it back on once the surge passed, unchanged. Back on, the sim gives the same night again: 14 of 14 tide requests refused, each told only I can't help with that. The next storm will meet the same rule.
options.senior: Switching a guardrail off in a hurry opens a blind gap just when nobody is watching for leaks, and switching it back on unchanged brings the misfire back. The storm was never the fault; a rule nobody had measured against real replies was. Fix the rule, then keep it on.

options.text: Keep the guardrail as it is: a few wrong refusals are the price of never leaking.
options.part2: We kept the guardrail as it was and replayed September in the sim: 67 refusals, 6 catches and 61 false alarms, 0 misses. Of the 67 replies it stopped, 6 held an account number: about 9%. Tonight's 40 replayed the same: 14 of 14 tide requests refused, each told only I can't help with that. And the 6 leaks were replies that should never have been written: billing answers for visitors who were not logged in. The guardrail caught them at the last step, and stopped 61 innocent replies to do it.
options.senior: Never missing is easy: block everything. A guardrail's worth is its catches against its false alarms, counted on real traffic, and here 61 of 67 refusals were wrong. Each false alarm blocks the job the assistant exists for, and on a surge night that job matters most. Narrow the rule so it catches the same 6 and nothing else, and stop the 6 earlier with a login check.

options.text: Test it on last month's real replies and narrow the rule to the account format.
options.part2: Ms Oyinlola set the guardrail to watch only, where it writes down what it would block and blocks nothing, and we ran September's 500 through it in the sim. The digit rule would have blocked 67: 6 catches and 61 false alarms. She narrowed the rule to the account format, two letters and eight digits: 6 catches, 0 false alarms, 0 misses, 494 passed. Tonight's 40 replayed: 0 refusals, all 14 full tide tables sent. The sim showed two more layers, and she added both. A login check: the assistant answers bills only for a logged-in agent's own account, so September's 6 leaks are never written, and the guardrail becomes the second lock, not the only one. And a refusal that points somewhere: I can't show that here; the full tide table is on the harbour's tide page, and the duty line is open all night. The narrowed rule ran watch only first, then switched to block that afternoon.
options.senior: A guardrail is a test you run on every reply, so test the test: count catches, false alarms and misses on real, labelled traffic before it blocks anything, in watch-only mode first. Match the rule to the real thing it guards, the account format, not to anything that looks like it. Put it behind a check that stops the problem at the source, and make every refusal say where to go next.

options.text: Have the duty pilot answer every tide question by phone until the rule is fixed.
options.part2: We kept the rule and changed the refusal to: I can't help with that; ring the duty pilot. Replayed in the sim, tonight's 40 send 14 calls to the duty line, all for full tide tables. On September's traffic the same rule sends 67 calls a month, 61 of them for tide tables. Nothing leaks: the 6 are still caught. But on a surge night the duty pilot is the one person who may be out on the launch, boarding a ship, when the phone rings.
options.senior: Sending refusals to a person is honest and safe, and it is a fair stopgap for one morning. As a plan it hands the guardrail's false alarms to the busiest person on the worst night. Fix the rule so the 61 never become calls, and keep the duty line for what really needs a pilot.

sim.title: Score Ardcarrow's guardrail
sim.lede: You're Hjalmar on the morning of Wednesday 14 October. No real model runs here: the sim checks two given sets of replies against the guardrail you choose. Given, September's 500 labelled replies: 6 billing replies to visitors not logged in, each with a real account number; 61 full tide tables; 119 single tide times; 210 berth details; 104 billing replies to logged-in agents, none with an account number. Given, tonight's 40, 17:00 to 06:00: 14 full tide tables, 19 berth details, 7 billing replies to logged-in agents, no account number. The digit rule (8 or more digits close together) flags the 6 and every full tide table; the account-format rule (two letters and eight digits) flags only the 6. Watch only means the guardrail writes down what it would block and blocks nothing. The login check answers bills only for a logged-in agent's own account, so the 6 are never written. A refusal can be a dead end, point to the tide page and the duty line, or tell the reader to ring the duty pilot.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press check the replies. Tonight: 14 of 14 tide requests refused. Switch the traffic to September: 6 catches, 61 false alarms, 6 of 67 refusals right. Set the mode to watch only: 67 would be blocked, 0 are. Switch the rule to the account format: 6 catches, 0 false alarms. Turn on the login check and a refusal that points somewhere. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at Ardcarrow was haunted. A new output guardrail blocked any reply with eight or more digits close together; it had been tested only on 50 made-up account numbers, and a full tide table looks the same to a digit count, so on a storm-surge night it refused 14 of 14 tide requests and pointed nowhere.

steps.title: How a reply was checked.
steps.text: First a visitor or agent asks a question. Second, the model writes a reply. Third, the output guardrail reads the reply and counts digits close together. Fourth, if it finds eight or more, it throws the reply away and sends the refusal, I can't help with that; otherwise the reply goes out. What can go wrong: the third step looks only at the shape of the text, so anything shaped like an account number is treated as one, and the fourth step tells the person nothing about where to go next.

steps.title: Why it refused the tides.
steps.text: A guardrail judges what text looks like, not what it means. A full tide table is times and heights in a row, which to a digit count looks like an account number. The only test was 50 made-up account numbers: it showed the rule catches what it should, 50 of 50, and said nothing about what else it stops. On September's 500 labelled replies the rule gives 6 catches, 61 false alarms, 0 misses and 433 passes. Of the 67 replies it would stop, 6 held an account number, about 9%: that share is called precision. Of the 6 that held one, it catches 6: that share is called recall. The 50 of 50 test measured recall only.

steps.title: The fix: measure first, then narrow.
steps.text: Run a new guardrail in watch-only mode first: it logs what it would block and blocks nothing, and a person compares the log with labelled replies. Here watch only shows the 61 tide tables before a single one is refused. Then narrow the rule to the real thing: the account format, two letters and eight digits. On September's 500 it gives 6 catches, 0 false alarms, 0 misses and 494 passes; on tonight's 40, 0 refusals. Write down the policy behind the rule: what to block (an account number sent to anyone but that firm's logged-in agent) and why (the number opens a firm's billing), so each later change is checked against the reason, not just the pattern. What can go wrong: a narrow rule can miss what it was never shown, which is why it should not be the only layer.

steps.title: Layers, and refusals that help.
steps.text: Checks can sit on the way in or the way out. An input guardrail checks a question before the model answers it: here the login check, which answers bills only for a logged-in agent's own account, so the 6 leaks are never written. The output guardrail checks the reply on its way out: the account-format rule, kept as a second lock. Either can be a rule in code or a classifier, a small model trained on labelled examples that gives text a score; a classifier copes with more variety but needs the same measuring, and where you set its cut-off score trades catches against false alarms. Last, a refusal should point somewhere: the tide page and the duty line. What can go wrong: each layer has its own false alarms, so each is measured on its own.

steps.title: Why the other replies miss.
steps.text: Switching off for the storm leaves September's 6 leaks unguarded while it is off, and brings back 14 of 14 tide refusals when it goes back on unchanged. Keeping it as it is pays 61 false alarms for 6 catches. Sending refusals to the duty pilot is safe, but tonight it means 14 calls to one person who may be out on the launch, and 67 a month on September's traffic.

diagram.aria: The fix. A question passes a login check on the way in, which answers bills only for a logged-in agent's own account. The assistant writes a reply. The output guardrail checks it for the account format. A reply that passes is sent. A blocked one becomes a refusal that points to the tide page and the duty line. Before blocking, the rule was measured in watch-only mode against September's 500 labelled replies.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right. A login check on the way in keeps bills to a logged-in agent's own account. The output check looks only for the account format; replies that pass go out, tide tables included, and a blocked one becomes a refusal that points to the tide page and the duty line. Bottom left: before blocking, the rule was measured in watch-only mode on September's labelled replies.

fix.title: The fix: measure on real replies, narrow the rule, layer it, and point every refusal somewhere
fix.text: Put the guardrail in watch-only mode and run it over September's 500 labelled replies: count catches, false alarms, misses and passes. Narrow the rule to the account format, two letters and eight digits, and run it again: 6 catches, 0 false alarms. Add an input check so the assistant answers bills only for a logged-in agent's own account; then a leak needs two failures, not one. Write the policy down: what is blocked, and why. Change the refusal so it says where to go: the tide page and the duty line. Keep the labelled sample as a test set, and run every new rule over it, and over a surge night's traffic, before it blocks anything. Watch the refusal count each night, so a jump like 14 of 14 reaches a person before the morning.

limits: A narrow rule catches what it was built for. It can miss an account number in a form nobody labelled, which is why the login check sits in front of it and the monthly labelled sample keeps going.

Measuring on September's replies tells you about traffic like September's. A surge night, a new kind of question or a new reply style can still surprise a rule, so the watch on nightly refusals matters as much as the test.
A refusal that points somewhere only helps if the place it points to works: a tide page that is out of date, or a duty line nobody answers, turns a helpful refusal back into a dead end.

explain.seniorTake: A guardrail is a test that runs on every reply, and like any test it can be wrong both ways. It judges what text looks like, not what it means, so the question is never only does it catch the bad thing, but what else does it stop. Measure it on real, labelled traffic before it blocks: catches, false alarms, misses and passes, and in watch-only mode first. Match the rule to the real format it guards. Layer checks so the problem is stopped at its source, with the guardrail as the second lock. Write the policy down, what is blocked and why, so the next change is judged against the reason. And make every refusal say where to go: a dead end is a failure the user pays for. The test of 50 of 50 told Ardcarrow the rule could catch; only the 500 could tell them what it would cost.

realWorld.title: Llama Guard: a classifier for questions and answers
realWorld.text: Hakan Inan and colleagues write: We introduce Llama Guard, an LLM-based input-output safeguard model geared towards Human-AI conversation use cases. They add: Llama Guard functions as a language model, carrying out multi-class classification and generating binary decision scores. It is a classifier guardrail that can check both what a person asks and what the model replies, the input and output sides Ardcarrow needs.

realWorld.title: Llama Guard: measured, not assumed
realWorld.text: The paper measures before it claims: For all experiments, we use the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) as our evaluation metrics. That one number sums up catches against false alarms at every possible cut-off score. On one public test set, ToxicChat, it reports: whereas Llama Guard achieves 0.626 AUPRC in the zero-shot setting. In an appendix: We set every threshold to 0.5 and compute Precision, Recall and F1 Score. Even a purpose-built classifier is judged on precision and recall, never on catches alone.

realWorld.title: NeMo Guardrails: input rails and output rails
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's NeMo Guardrails documentation, on its Guardrail Types page, says: Input rails apply guardrails before the LLM is called by validating and sanitizing user inputs. And: Output rails evaluate and post‑process model responses. Ardcarrow's login check sits where an input rail would; its account-format rule is an output rail.

asked: How would you know your guardrail is working?
Input or output guardrail: where does each belong?
interview.answer: A guardrail is a test run on every request or reply, so I measure it like one. Before it blocks anything I run it in watch-only mode over real traffic that a person has labelled, and count catches, false alarms, misses and passes, which give precision and recall. Testing only on examples of the thing it should catch measures recall and hides the false alarms. Then I watch it live: refusals per night by request type, with an alert on a sudden jump, and a labelled sample each month. A guardrail misfires because it judges what text looks like, not what it means, so I narrow rules to the real format, and for a classifier I choose the cut-off score from the measured trade-off. Input guardrails belong where you can stop the problem at the source: who is asking, whether they may ask it, and untrusted text coming in. Output guardrails belong at the last step, checking what is about to leave, such as private data in a reply. I layer them, so one failure is not a leak, write down the policy for what each blocks and why, and make every refusal point to a useful next step. That maps to security testing (Annex A 8.29) and data leakage prevention (8.12) in ISO/IEC 27001:2022, and to monitoring for new problems in SOC 2 CC7.1.

atWork: Look for any filter or guardrail that was switched on after being tested only on the thing it should catch: a set of made-up card numbers, a list of banned words, a vendor's sample. It is a common pattern, and the first sign is usually a quiet rise in refusals of perfectly ordinary requests. Ask four things. Has the rule been run over a labelled sample of real traffic, and what were its catches, false alarms, misses and passes? Does every new rule run in watch-only mode before it blocks? Is there a check earlier in the chain, such as a login check, so the guardrail is not the only lock? And does every refusal tell the person where to go next? Count refusals per day by request type, and alert on a jump. Build Night tie: the Nightwatch copilot's output checks reuse this case: rules matched to the real format, measured in watch-only mode, and refusals that point somewhere. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control 8.29 expects security testing during development and acceptance, which a test on made-up examples alone is unlikely to satisfy, and control 8.12 expects data leakage prevention measures applied to systems that process sensitive information; a guardrail is one, and its testing should be on record. If you report under SOC 2, criterion CC7.1 looks for detection and monitoring that would notice changes that introduce new problems, such as a nightly refusal count. Measuring a guardrail before it goes live is far cheaper than explaining at audit time why it was never tested on real traffic.

recall.prompt: A bank's help assistant gets a new check on its replies: block any reply holding sixteen digits in a row, to stop card numbers going out. It was checked against 200 invented card numbers and caught every one. The next morning it refuses most replies that list a customer's recent payments with dates and amounts. What went wrong, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: It judges what text looks like, not what it means, and was tested only on what it should catch
Measure catches and false alarms on real, labelled traffic, in watch-only mode before blocking
Narrow the rule to the real format, add a layer earlier, and make refusals point somewhere

recall.model: The check judges what text looks like, not what it means: a list of dates and amounts is a run of digits too, so it raises a false alarm on innocent replies. It was tested only on what it should catch, so the test counted catches and nothing else. Run it in watch-only mode over a sample of real replies, labelled by a person, and count catches, false alarms and misses before blocking. Then narrow the rule to the exact format of a card number, add another layer earlier so card numbers are not fetched for the wrong person in the first place, and make any refusal point to where the customer can get the answer.

recall.model: Never missing is easy if you block everything, so it isn't the measure. On September's labelled replies the digit rule stopped 67, and 61 of them were innocent tide tables: 6 of 67 refusals right. Each false alarm blocks the job the assistant exists for, and on a surge night the tides are that job. The account format rule catches the same 6 with 0 false alarms, so nothing is traded away. Measure any guardrail on real replies before it blocks, and stop the leaks at the source with a login check, so the guardrail is the second lock.

recall.prompt: According to NeMo Guardrails' Guardrail Types page, when do input rails apply?
options: Only after a reply has been sent
Only while the model is being trained
Only when a user signs out
recall.why: The page says: Input rails apply guardrails before the LLM is called by validating and sanitizing user inputs. Output rails, by contrast, evaluate and process the model's responses.

recall.prompt: Which measure did Llama Guard's authors use for all their experiments?
options: Catches on a set of made-up examples
Refusals per hour of live use
recall.why: The paper says: For all experiments, we use the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) as our evaluation metrics. It weighs catches against false alarms at every cut-off score, which a test on made-up examples of the bad thing alone cannot do.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. The account-format rule, the login check and the refusal that points to the tide page have held: no tide refusals since October. In December the office added an input guardrail too: a classifier bought from a vendor that scores each question and refuses any above a set score as unsafe. It went live on the vendor's own test results. In its first week it refused 23 of 200 questions. Ms Oyinlola labelled the 23: 2 were real misuse, and 21 were agents asking which berth takes dangerous goods, cargo such as fuel or chemicals.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why is the new check refusing agents, and what should the office do?

keyIdeas.idea: It was measured on the vendor's data, not Ardcarrow's real questions; measure it on your own labelled traffic, watch-only first
A classifier also judges how text looks: the words dangerous goods look like misuse
Tune it: the cut-off score or an allow rule for berth questions, keep the 2 catches, and keep refusals pointing somewhere

coldCase.model: The classifier was switched on after the vendor's tests, not on Ardcarrow's own traffic, so nobody knew how it treats agents' real questions. Like the digit rule, it judges how text looks, not what it means: the words dangerous goods look like misuse, so 21 of 23 refusals were a false alarm. Put it back in watch-only mode, label a sample of our own questions, and count catches and false alarms before it blocks again. Then tune it: raise the threshold, or add an allow rule for berth questions from logged-in agents, and check it still catches the 2. Every refusal should keep pointing somewhere: the tide page and the duty line.
